Because it cuts the root of the bases by appropriately realizing the two forms of selflessness, it is the knowledge of the bases. Regarding this, out of two aspects, the pitfall or discordant class is the knowledge of the bases of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and by illustrating and teaching its antidote to be the knowledge of the bases of the Mahāyāna, one practices in the manner of cutting off the pitfall of the inferior vehicle. There are nine phenomena that illustrate this; moreover, as it says, "Through knowledge one does not dwell in existence, / and through compassion one does not dwell in peace; / the discordant class and their antidotes, / application and its equality, / and the path of seeing of the śrāvakas and so forth; / such is asserted as the very knowledge of all." Through this, these subdivisions by minor topics are also incidentally complete; they should be known extensively elsewhere.

The essence of the third topic, the knowledge of the bases that knows all, is the realization of the non-apprehension of the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense sources, which have become the supports for the basis and path. Because it is the basis for the arising of superimpositions and the basis for the cutting of superimpositions, it is called the knowledge of the bases. Because it cuts the root of the bases by appropriately realizing the two forms of selflessness, it is the knowledge of the bases. Regarding this, out of two aspects, the pitfall or discordant class is the knowledge of the bases of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and by illustrating and teaching its antidote to be the knowledge of the bases of the Mahāyāna, one practices in the manner of cutting off the pitfall of the inferior vehicle. There are nine phenomena that illustrate this; moreover, as it says, "Through knowledge one does not dwell in existence, / and through compassion one does not dwell in peace; / the discordant class and their antidotes, / application and its equality, / and the path of seeing of the śrāvakas and so forth; / such is asserted as the very knowledge of all." Through this, these subdivisions by minor topics are also incidentally complete; they should be known extensively elsewhere.

Regarding this from "how the hero practices" up to "moves about": Moreover, by the power of the hero, the bodhisattva, practicing in whatever way through various methods, and of the perfection of wisdom, they have perfectly transcended the two afflictions that are the causes of the three realms, yet they are not liberated in the manner of the one-sided peace of the śrāvakas. Even though the afflictions of ignorance and views are eliminated, without abandoning even the mere contaminants of desire and craving, they demonstrate birth through skillful means. Likewise for the example, even though they lack aging, sickness, and death, they demonstrate dying and transmigrating and so forth in the perception of the beings to be tamed. These wandering beings who lack such wisdom are attached to the aggregates that are the basis of name, namely the four of feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness, and the aggregate of form—they are attached to those which are like the mud of the five aggregates, difficult to emerge from. For example, just as a continuous bucket water-wheel is moved by the wind, the meaning is that they wander again and again in the wheel of saṃsāra, in the three realms and the six classes of beings. Knowing that those wanderers who are mistaken about the path do not escape from saṃsāra because they are caught in the snare of the four rivers, similarly to the example of a deer caught in a snare that does not escape, the one endowed with the wisdom that knows non-apprehension "moves about" without adhering to or depending upon anything whatsoever, like a bird flying in the sky.

Thus it is said: Regarding this from "perfectly pure practice" up to "goes without attachment": if some bodhisattva with perfectly pure practice does not practice by adhering to the object of form, and similarly does not practice by way of adhering to consciousness, perception, feeling, and volition, then practicing in that way without adherence completely abandons all attachment and aversion, and that intellect going away from attachment and adherence is the Sugatas' practice of wisdom. Practicing in that way by way of not adhering to the five aggregates as appearing to be true, that bodhisattva is skilled because they possess the momentum of training, and being brilliant by realizing the meaning, having severed attachment and adherence from their own continuum, they "go" to the stage of buddhahood without attachment and adherence even to the wandering beings of the three realms.

Work: འཕགས་པ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་ཊཱི་ཀ་ཡིད་བཞིན་གྱི་ནོར་བུ་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་ལྟ་བུ་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རྒྱ་མཚོའི་སྡེ། (Commentaries on the Short Prajnaparamita Sutras:The Ocean of Perfection.), author: null. [2-87] source:
གཟུགས་ཀྱི་དག་པ་ཞེས་པ་ནས། དབྱེར་མེད་གཅད་དུ་མེད་ཞེས་བར་ལ། ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཡུལ་ནི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པ་སྟེ། ཡུལ་ནི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་དག་པ་སྐྱེས་བུ་ཟུང་བཞི་འབྲས་བུ་དག་དང་རིག་པར་བྱའོ། །དེ་ལྟར་འབྲས་བུ་བཞི་དག་དཔེ་དང་ཆོས་ཅན་གཟུགས་དག་པ་དང༌། ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་འབྲས་བུ་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པ་ཉིད་དག་པར་གསུངས་ལ། དེ་ལྟར་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པ་ཉིད་དག་པ་དང༌། འབྲས་བུ་བཞི་དག་པ་དང་ཆོས་ཅན་གཟུགས་དག་པ་གསུམ་པོ་ལ་ཐ་དད་མེད་པའི་དཔེ་ནི། ནམ་མཁའི་ཁམས་དང་མཚུངས་ཏེ་དངོས་པོ་ལ་དབྱེར་མེད་ཅིང་བློས་ཀྱང་ཐ་དད་དུ་གཅད་དུ་མེད་དོ། །དེ་ཡན་ཆད་ཀྱི་ལམ་ཤེས་བཤད་ནས།

Regarding this from "purity of form" up to "indivisible and uncuttable": the object of wisdom is the lack of nature of all phenomena; the object is to be known as the purity of form and the pure results of the four pairs of persons. Thus, it is taught that the four pure results are the example, and the pure subject form and the pure result of the Mahāyāna, omniscience, are pure. Thus, the example for there being no difference among those three—the purity of omniscience, the purity of the four results, and the purity of the subject form—is that they are like the element of space: indivisible in entity and also uncuttable into distinctions by the intellect. Having explained knowledge of the path up to that point,

[2-88] source:
སྐབས་གསུམ་པ་ཀུན་ཤེས་པའི་གཞི་ཤེས་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ནི། གཞི་ལམ་དུ་བརྟེན་དུ་གྱུར་པའི་ཕུང་པོ་ཁམས་དང་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་མི་དམིགས་པར་རྟོགས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། སྒྲོ་འདོགས་སྐྱེ་བའི་གཞི་དང༌། སྒྲོ་འདོགས་གཅད་པའི་གཞི་ཡིན་པས་གཞི་ཤེས་བྱ། དེ་བདག་མེད་གཉིས་ཅི་རིགས་པར་རྟོགས་པས་གཞི་རྩ་ཆོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་གཞི་ཤེས་ཡིན་ནོ། །འདི་ལ་གཉིས་ལས་གོལ་ས་མི་མཐུན་ཕྱོགས་ཉན་རང་གི་གཞི་ཤེས་ཡིན་ལ། དེ་གཉེན་པོ་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་གཞི་ཤེས་ཡིན་པར་མཚོན་ནས་བསྟན་པས་ཐེག་དམན་གྱི་གོལ་ས་བཅད་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པའོ། །འདི་ལ་མཚོན་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཆོས་དགུ་ཡོད་དེ།དེ་ཡང༌།ཤེས་པས་སྲིད་ལ་མི་གནས་ཤིང༌། །སྙིང་རྗེས་ཞི་ལ་མི་གནས་དང༌། །མི་མཐུན་གཉེན་པོ་ཕྱོགས་དག་དང༌། །སྦྱོར་དང་དེའི་མཉམ་ཉིད་དང༌། །ཉན་ཐོས་ལ་སོགས་མཐོང་བའི་ལམ། །དེ་འདྲ་ཀུན་ཤེས་ཉིད་དུ་འདོད། །ཞེས་པས་སྐབས་ཕྲན་གྱིས་ཕྱེ་བ་འདི་དག་ཀྱང་ཞོར་ལ་ཚང་བ་ཡིན་ཏེ། རྒྱས་པར་གཞན་དུ་ཤེས་སོ། །

The essence of the third topic, the knowledge of the bases that knows all, is the realization of the non-apprehension of the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense sources, which have become the supports for the basis and path. Because it is the basis for the arising of superimpositions and the basis for the cutting of superimpositions, it is called the knowledge of the bases. Because it cuts the root of the bases by appropriately realizing the two forms of selflessness, it is the knowledge of the bases. Regarding this, out of two aspects, the pitfall or discordant class is the knowledge of the bases of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and by illustrating and teaching its antidote to be the knowledge of the bases of the Mahāyāna, one practices in the manner of cutting off the pitfall of the inferior vehicle. There are nine phenomena that illustrate this; moreover, as it says, "Through knowledge one does not dwell in existence, / and through compassion one does not dwell in peace; / the discordant class and their antidotes, / application and its equality, / and the path of seeing of the śrāvakas and so forth; / such is asserted as the very knowledge of all." Through this, these subdivisions by minor topics are also incidentally complete; they should be known extensively elsewhere.

[2-90] source:
དཔའ་བོ་གར་སྤྱོད་ཅེས་པ་ནས། རྣམ་པར་རྒྱུ་ཞེས་པའི་བར་གྱིས། དེ་ཡང་དཔའ་བོ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གར་ལྟར་ཐབས་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱིས་སྤྱོད་པ་དང་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་མཐུ་ཡིས། ཁམས་གསུམ་གྱི་རྒྱུ་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་གཉིས་ལས་ཡང་དག་པར་འདས་ལ་ཉན་ཐོས་ཞི་བ་ཕྱོགས་གཅིག་པ་ལྟར་དུ་རྣམ་པར་གྲོལ་བའང་མིན། མ་རིག་པ་དང་ལྟ་བའི་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་བཙལ་བར་གྱུར་ཀྱང་འདོད་པ་དང་སྲེད་པའི་ཟག་པ་ཙམ་ཡང་མ་སྤངས་པར་ཐབས་མཁས་ཀྱི་སྐྱེ་བ་ལྟར་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་ཅིང༌། དཔེ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་རྒ་བ་དང་ན་བ་དང་འཆི་བ་མེད་ཀྱང་གདུལ་བྱའི་བློ་ངོར་འཆི་འཕོ་ལ་སོགས་ཡོད་པ་ལྟར་སྟོན། དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་ཤེས་རབ་མེད་པའི་འགྲོ་བ་འདི་དག་ནི་མིང་གཞིའི་ཕུང་པོ་སྟེ། ཚོར་བ་དང་འདུ་ཤེས་འདུ་བྱེད་རྣམ་ཤེས་བཞི་དང་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་སྟེ། ཕུང་པོ་ལྔའི་འདམ་ལྟར་ཐོན་དཀའ་བ་དེ་དག་ལ་ཆགས་ཤིང༌། དཔེར་ན་རླུང་གིས་བསྐྱོད་པའི་ཟོ་ཆུ་ཁྱུད་མོའི་འཁོར་ལོ་ལྟ་བུའི་དོན་འཁོར་བའི་འཁོར་ལོ་ཁམས་གསུམ་དང་རིགས་དྲུག་ཏུ་ཡང་དང་ཡང་དུ་འཁྱམ། འགྲོ་བ་ལམ་ལ་འཁྲུལ་པ་རྣམས་དཔེར་ན་རི་དྭགས་རྒྱར་ཆུད་པ་དེ་མི་ཐར་པ་དེ་དང་འདྲ་བར་ཆུ་བོ་བཞིའི་རྒྱར་ཆུད་པས་འཁོར་བ་ལས་མི་ཐར་བར་ཤེས་ནས། མི་དམིགས་པར་ཤེས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དེ་ནམ་མཁའ་ལ་བྱ་འཕུར་བ་བཞིན་དུ་གང་ལ་ཡང་མ་ཞེན་ཅིང་མི་བརྟེན་པར་རྣམ་པར་རྒྱུས་སོ། །

Regarding this from "how the hero practices" up to "moves about": Moreover, by the power of the hero, the bodhisattva, practicing in whatever way through various methods, and of the perfection of wisdom, they have perfectly transcended the two afflictions that are the causes of the three realms, yet they are not liberated in the manner of the one-sided peace of the śrāvakas. Even though the afflictions of ignorance and views are eliminated, without abandoning even the mere contaminants of desire and craving, they demonstrate birth through skillful means. Likewise for the example, even though they lack aging, sickness, and death, they demonstrate dying and transmigrating and so forth in the perception of the beings to be tamed. These wandering beings who lack such wisdom are attached to the aggregates that are the basis of name, namely the four of feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness, and the aggregate of form—they are attached to those which are like the mud of the five aggregates, difficult to emerge from. For example, just as a continuous bucket water-wheel is moved by the wind, the meaning is that they wander again and again in the wheel of saṃsāra, in the three realms and the six classes of beings. Knowing that those wanderers who are mistaken about the path do not escape from saṃsāra because they are caught in the snare of the four rivers, similarly to the example of a deer caught in a snare that does not escape, the one endowed with the wisdom that knows non-apprehension "moves about" without adhering to or depending upon anything whatsoever, like a bird flying in the sky.

Thus it is said: Regarding this from "perfectly pure practice" up to "goes without attachment": if some bodhisattva with perfectly pure practice does not practice by adhering to the object of form, and similarly does not practice by way of adhering to consciousness, perception, feeling, and volition, then practicing in that way without adherence completely abandons all attachment and aversion, and that intellect going away from attachment and adherence is the Sugatas' practice of wisdom. Practicing in that way by way of not adhering to the five aggregates as appearing to be true, that bodhisattva is skilled because they possess the momentum of training, and being brilliant by realizing the meaning, having severed attachment and adherence from their own continuum, they "go" to the stage of buddhahood without attachment and adherence even to the wandering beings of the three realms.

heading: **དྲི་བ་སྔོན་དུ་འགྲོ་བས་ཤེས་རབ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: Applying to wisdom preceded by a question: Of the two—the complete training in all aspects and the culmination training, which mainly teach meditative equipoise as the object of meditation for the method of practicing the meaning of the three knowledges—the essence of the fourth topic, the application of complete training in all aspects, is bringing the realization of the three knowledges into the domain of effort by meditating on the four causes of the dharmakāya by subsuming the three paths into objects of observation. Because the four applications are taught by way of their own essences, they do not need to be taught by illustration. Regarding this, it is taught through eleven divisions, and furthermore it is also taught by these minor topics: "The aspects along with the applications, / the qualities, faults, and characteristics, / the factors conducive to liberation and conducive to penetration, / the assembly of irreversible learners, / the equality of existence and peace, / the unsurpassed pure realms, / and the complete realization of all aspects— / this is along with skillful means." By saying this, although there is no explicit demarcation, they are implicitly complete.

The essence of the third topic, the knowledge of the bases that knows all, is the realization of the non-apprehension of the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense sources, which have become the supports for the basis and path. Because it is the basis for the arising of superimpositions and the basis for the cutting of superimpositions, it is called the knowledge of the bases. Because it cuts the root of the bases by appropriately realizing the two forms of selflessness, it is the knowledge of the bases. Regarding this, out of two aspects, the pitfall or discordant class is the knowledge of the bases of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and by illustrating and teaching its antidote to be the knowledge of the bases of the Mahāyāna, one practices in the manner of cutting off the pitfall of the inferior vehicle. There are nine phenomena that illustrate this; moreover, as it says, "Through knowledge one does not dwell in existence, / and through compassion one does not dwell in peace; / the discordant class and their antidotes, / application and its equality, / and the path of seeing of the śrāvakas and so forth; / such is asserted as the very knowledge of all." Through this, these subdivisions by minor topics are also incidentally complete; they should be known extensively elsewhere.

Regarding this from "how the hero practices" up to "moves about": Moreover, by the power of the hero, the bodhisattva, practicing in whatever way through various methods, and of the perfection of wisdom, they have perfectly transcended the two afflictions that are the causes of the three realms, yet they are not liberated in the manner of the one-sided peace of the śrāvakas. Even though the afflictions of ignorance and views are eliminated, without abandoning even the mere contaminants of desire and craving, they demonstrate birth through skillful means. Likewise for the example, even though they lack aging, sickness, and death, they demonstrate dying and transmigrating and so forth in the perception of the beings to be tamed. These wandering beings who lack such wisdom are attached to the aggregates that are the basis of name, namely the four of feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness, and the aggregate of form—they are attached to those which are like the mud of the five aggregates, difficult to emerge from. For example, just as a continuous bucket water-wheel is moved by the wind, the meaning is that they wander again and again in the wheel of saṃsāra, in the three realms and the six classes of beings. Knowing that those wanderers who are mistaken about the path do not escape from saṃsāra because they are caught in the snare of the four rivers, similarly to the example of a deer caught in a snare that does not escape, the one endowed with the wisdom that knows non-apprehension "moves about" without adhering to or depending upon anything whatsoever, like a bird flying in the sky.

Thus it is said: Regarding this from "perfectly pure practice" up to "goes without attachment": if some bodhisattva with perfectly pure practice does not practice by adhering to the object of form, and similarly does not practice by way of adhering to consciousness, perception, feeling, and volition, then practicing in that way without adherence completely abandons all attachment and aversion, and that intellect going away from attachment and adherence is the Sugatas' practice of wisdom. Practicing in that way by way of not adhering to the five aggregates as appearing to be true, that bodhisattva is skilled because they possess the momentum of training, and being brilliant by realizing the meaning, having severed attachment and adherence from their own continuum, they "go" to the stage of buddhahood without attachment and adherence even to the wandering beings of the three realms.

heading: **དྲི་བ་སྔོན་དུ་འགྲོ་བས་ཤེས་རབ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: Thus it is said: Regarding this from "To the Victor" up to "the bodhisattva exerts": the lord of gods, Śakra, requested to the Victor, Śākyamuni: "Bhagavān, how should a bodhisattva, a great being, who wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom, exert themselves? How should they train in the basis of application of non-application?" Having been requested this, in reply to that: they do not exert themselves even an atom in any phenomenon such as the aggregates, elements, and sense sources, and that non-exertion in the aggregates and so forth is the exertion of the bodhisattva.

Regarding this from "how the hero practices" up to "moves about": Moreover, by the power of the hero, the bodhisattva, practicing in whatever way through various methods, and of the perfection of wisdom, they have perfectly transcended the two afflictions that are the causes of the three realms, yet they are not liberated in the manner of the one-sided peace of the śrāvakas. Even though the afflictions of ignorance and views are eliminated, without abandoning even the mere contaminants of desire and craving, they demonstrate birth through skillful means. Likewise for the example, even though they lack aging, sickness, and death, they demonstrate dying and transmigrating and so forth in the perception of the beings to be tamed. These wandering beings who lack such wisdom are attached to the aggregates that are the basis of name, namely the four of feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness, and the aggregate of form—they are attached to those which are like the mud of the five aggregates, difficult to emerge from. For example, just as a continuous bucket water-wheel is moved by the wind, the meaning is that they wander again and again in the wheel of saṃsāra, in the three realms and the six classes of beings. Knowing that those wanderers who are mistaken about the path do not escape from saṃsāra because they are caught in the snare of the four rivers, similarly to the example of a deer caught in a snare that does not escape, the one endowed with the wisdom that knows non-apprehension "moves about" without adhering to or depending upon anything whatsoever, like a bird flying in the sky.

Thus it is said: Regarding this from "perfectly pure practice" up to "goes without attachment": if some bodhisattva with perfectly pure practice does not practice by adhering to the object of form, and similarly does not practice by way of adhering to consciousness, perception, feeling, and volition, then practicing in that way without adherence completely abandons all attachment and aversion, and that intellect going away from attachment and adherence is the Sugatas' practice of wisdom. The essence of the third topic, the knowledge of the bases that knows all, is the realization of the non-apprehension of the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense sources, which have become the supports for the basis and path. Because it is the basis for the arising of superimpositions and the basis for the cutting of superimpositions, it is called the knowledge of the bases. Because it cuts the root of the bases by appropriately realizing the two forms of selflessness, it is the knowledge of the bases. Regarding this, out of two aspects, the pitfall or discordant class is the knowledge of the bases of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and by illustrating and teaching its antidote to be the knowledge of the bases of the Mahāyāna, one practices in the manner of cutting off the pitfall of the inferior vehicle. There are nine phenomena that illustrate this; moreover, as it says, "Through knowledge one does not dwell in existence, / and through compassion one does not dwell in peace; / the discordant class and their antidotes, / application and its equality, / and the path of seeing of the śrāvakas and so forth; / such is asserted as the very knowledge of all." Through this, these subdivisions by minor topics are also incidentally complete; they should be known extensively elsewhere.

Regarding this from "how the hero practices" up to "moves about": Moreover, by the power of the hero, the bodhisattva, practicing in whatever way through various methods, and of the perfection of wisdom, they have perfectly transcended the two afflictions that are the causes of the three realms, yet they are not liberated in the manner of the one-sided peace of the śrāvakas. Even though the afflictions of ignorance and views are eliminated, without abandoning even the mere contaminants of desire and craving, they demonstrate birth through skillful means. Likewise for the example, even though they lack aging, sickness, and death, they demonstrate dying and transmigrating and so forth in the perception of the beings to be tamed. These wandering beings who lack such wisdom are attached to the aggregates that are the basis of name, namely the four of feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness, and the aggregate of form—they are attached to those which are like the mud of the five aggregates, difficult to emerge from. For example, just as a continuous bucket water-wheel is moved by the wind, the meaning is that they wander again and again in the wheel of saṃsāra, in the three realms and the six classes of beings. Knowing that those wanderers who are mistaken about the path do not escape from saṃsāra because they are caught in the snare of the four rivers, similarly to the example of a deer caught in a snare that does not escape, the one endowed with the wisdom that knows non-apprehension "moves about" without adhering to or depending upon anything whatsoever, like a bird flying in the sky.

Thus it is said: Regarding this from "perfectly pure practice" up to "goes without attachment": if some bodhisattva with perfectly pure practice does not practice by adhering to the object of form, and similarly does not practice by way of adhering to consciousness, perception, feeling, and volition, then practicing in that way without adherence completely abandons all attachment and aversion, and that intellect going away from attachment and adherence is the Sugatas' practice of wisdom. Practicing in that way by way of not adhering to the five aggregates as appearing to be true, that bodhisattva is skilled because they possess the momentum of training, and being brilliant by realizing the meaning, having severed attachment and adherence from their own continuum, they "go" to the stage of buddhahood without attachment and adherence even to the wandering beings of the three realms.

heading: **སྦྱོར་བ་དེའི་སྔོན་དུ་འགྲོ་བའི་རྒྱུ་ཡོན་ཏན།**
translation: Regarding this from "whoever [knows] these phenomena" up to "and more": whichever person knows that all these phenomena of afflictive saṃsāra and all these phenomena of perfectly pure nirvāṇa appear like emanations and illusions but lack truth, and who has no doubt in that regard, thinking they are not like that and that one does not need to train, and who repeatedly engages in training in that way, that being is to be known as having already entered this path of the Mahāyāna since a long time in the past, and has previously made superior veneration to the objects, many koṭis of niyutas of perfectly and fully awakened Buddhas.

Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the root verses, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names in their standard Sanskrit forms (Subhūti, Śāriputra, Maitreya, Haribhadra) and technical terms recognisable (prajñāpāramitā = perfection of wisdom, bodhisattva). Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own.

གཟུགས་ཀྱི་དག་པ་ཞེས་པ་ནས། དབྱེར་མེད་གཅད་དུ་མེད་ཞེས་བར་ལ། ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཡུལ་ནི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པ་སྟེ། ཡུལ་ནི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་དག་པ་སྐྱེས་བུ་ཟུང་བཞི་འབྲས་བུ་དག་དང་རིག་པར་བྱའོ། །དེ་ལྟར་འབྲས་བུ་བཞི་དག་དཔེ་དང་ཆོས་ཅན་གཟུགས་དག་པ་དང༌། ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་འབྲས་བུ་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པ་ཉིད་དག་པར་གསུངས་ལ། དེ་ལྟར་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པ་ཉིད་དག་པ་དང༌། འབྲས་བུ་བཞི་དག་པ་དང་ཆོས་ཅན་གཟུགས་དག་པ་གསུམ་པོ་ལ་ཐ་དད་མེད་པའི་དཔེ་ནི། ནམ་མཁའི་ཁམས་དང་མཚུངས་ཏེ་དངོས་པོ་ལ་དབྱེར་མེད་ཅིང་བློས་ཀྱང་ཐ་དད་དུ་གཅད་དུ་མེད་དོ། །དེ་ཡན་ཆད་ཀྱི་ལམ་ཤེས་བཤད་ནས།

Regarding this from "purity of form" up to "indivisible and uncuttable": the object of wisdom is the lack of nature of all phenomena; the object is to be known as the purity of form and the pure results of the four pairs of persons. Thus, it is taught that the four pure results are the example, and the pure subject form and the pure result of the Mahāyāna, omniscience, are pure. Thus, the example for there being no difference among those three—the purity of omniscience, the purity of the four results, and the purity of the subject form—is that they are like the element of space: indivisible in entity and also uncuttable into distinctions by the intellect. Having explained knowledge of the path up to that point,

སྐབས་གསུམ་པ་ཀུན་ཤེས་པའི་གཞི་ཤེས་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ནི། གཞི་ལམ་དུ་བརྟེན་དུ་གྱུར་པའི་ཕུང་པོ་ཁམས་དང་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་མི་དམིགས་པར་རྟོགས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། སྒྲོ་འདོགས་སྐྱེ་བའི་གཞི་དང༌། སྒྲོ་འདོགས་གཅད་པའི་གཞི་ཡིན་པས་གཞི་ཤེས་བྱ། དེ་བདག་མེད་གཉིས་ཅི་རིགས་པར་རྟོགས་པས་གཞི་རྩ་ཆོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་གཞི་ཤེས་ཡིན་ནོ། །འདི་ལ་གཉིས་ལས་གོལ་ས་མི་མཐུན་ཕྱོགས་ཉན་རང་གི་གཞི་ཤེས་ཡིན་ལ། དེ་གཉེན་པོ་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་གཞི་ཤེས་ཡིན་པར་མཚོན་ནས་བསྟན་པས་ཐེག་དམན་གྱི་གོལ་ས་བཅད་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པའོ། །འདི་ལ་མཚོན་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཆོས་དགུ་ཡོད་དེ།དེ་ཡང༌།ཤེས་པས་སྲིད་ལ་མི་གནས་ཤིང༌། །སྙིང་རྗེས་ཞི་ལ་མི་གནས་དང༌། །མི་མཐུན་གཉེན་པོ་ཕྱོགས་དག་དང༌། །སྦྱོར་དང་དེའི་མཉམ་ཉིད་དང༌། །ཉན་ཐོས་ལ་སོགས་མཐོང་བའི་ལམ། །དེ་འདྲ་ཀུན་ཤེས་ཉིད་དུ་འདོད། །ཞེས་པས་སྐབས་ཕྲན་གྱིས་ཕྱེ་བ་འདི་དག་ཀྱང་ཞོར་ལ་ཚང་བ་ཡིན་ཏེ། རྒྱས་པར་གཞན་དུ་ཤེས་སོ། །

The essence of the third topic, the knowledge of the bases that knows all, is the realization of the non-apprehension of the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense sources, which have become the supports for the basis and path. Because it is the basis for the arising of superimpositions and the basis for the cutting of superimpositions, it is called the knowledge of the bases. Because it cuts the root of the bases by appropriately realizing the two forms of selflessness, it is the knowledge of the bases. Regarding this, out of two aspects, the pitfall or discordant class is the knowledge of the bases of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and by illustrating and teaching its antidote to be the knowledge of the bases of the Mahāyāna, one practices in the manner of cutting off the pitfall of the inferior vehicle. There are nine phenomena that illustrate this; moreover, as it says, "Through knowledge one does not dwell in existence, / and through compassion one does not dwell in peace; / the discordant class and their antidotes, / application and its equality, / and the path of seeing of the śrāvakas and so forth; / such is asserted as the very knowledge of all." Through this, these subdivisions by minor topics are also incidentally complete; they should be known extensively elsewhere.

དཔའ་བོ་གར་སྤྱོད་ཅེས་པ་ནས། རྣམ་པར་རྒྱུ་ཞེས་པའི་བར་གྱིས། དེ་ཡང་དཔའ་བོ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གར་ལྟར་ཐབས་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱིས་སྤྱོད་པ་དང་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་མཐུ་ཡིས། ཁམས་གསུམ་གྱི་རྒྱུ་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་གཉིས་ལས་ཡང་དག་པར་འདས་ལ་ཉན་ཐོས་ཞི་བ་ཕྱོགས་གཅིག་པ་ལྟར་དུ་རྣམ་པར་གྲོལ་བའང་མིན། མ་རིག་པ་དང་ལྟ་བའི་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་བཙལ་བར་གྱུར་ཀྱང་འདོད་པ་དང་སྲེད་པའི་ཟག་པ་ཙམ་ཡང་མ་སྤངས་པར་ཐབས་མཁས་ཀྱི་སྐྱེ་བ་ལྟར་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་ཅིང༌། དཔེ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་རྒ་བ་དང་ན་བ་དང་འཆི་བ་མེད་ཀྱང་གདུལ་བྱའི་བློ་ངོར་འཆི་འཕོ་ལ་སོགས་ཡོད་པ་ལྟར་སྟོན། དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་ཤེས་རབ་མེད་པའི་འགྲོ་བ་འདི་དག་ནི་མིང་གཞིའི་ཕུང་པོ་སྟེ། ཚོར་བ་དང་འདུ་ཤེས་འདུ་བྱེད་རྣམ་ཤེས་བཞི་དང་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་སྟེ། ཕུང་པོ་ལྔའི་འདམ་ལྟར་ཐོན་དཀའ་བ་དེ་དག་ལ་ཆགས་ཤིང༌། དཔེར་ན་རླུང་གིས་བསྐྱོད་པའི་ཟོ་ཆུ་ཁྱུད་མོའི་འཁོར་ལོ་ལྟ་བུའི་དོན་འཁོར་བའི་འཁོར་ལོ་ཁམས་གསུམ་དང་རིགས་དྲུག་ཏུ་ཡང་དང་ཡང་དུ་འཁྱམ། འགྲོ་བ་ལམ་ལ་འཁྲུལ་པ་རྣམས་དཔེར་ན་རི་དྭགས་རྒྱར་ཆུད་པ་དེ་མི་ཐར་པ་དེ་དང་འདྲ་བར་ཆུ་བོ་བཞིའི་རྒྱར་ཆུད་པས་འཁོར་བ་ལས་མི་ཐར་བར་ཤེས་ནས། མི་དམིགས་པར་ཤེས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དེ་ནམ་མཁའ་ལ་བྱ་འཕུར་བ་བཞིན་དུ་གང་ལ་ཡང་མ་ཞེན་ཅིང་མི་བརྟེན་པར་རྣམ་པར་རྒྱུས་སོ། །

Regarding this from "how the hero practices" up to "moves about": Moreover, by the power of the hero, the bodhisattva, practicing in whatever way through various methods, and of the perfection of wisdom, they have perfectly transcended the two afflictions that are the causes of the three realms, yet they are not liberated in the manner of the one-sided peace of the śrāvakas. Even though the afflictions of ignorance and views are eliminated, without abandoning even the mere contaminants of desire and craving, they demonstrate birth through skillful means. Likewise for the example, even though they lack aging, sickness, and death, they demonstrate dying and transmigrating and so forth in the perception of the beings to be tamed. These wandering beings who lack such wisdom are attached to the aggregates that are the basis of name, namely the four of feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness, and the aggregate of form—they are attached to those which are like the mud of the five aggregates, difficult to emerge from. For example, just as a continuous bucket water-wheel is moved by the wind, the meaning is that they wander again and again in the wheel of saṃsāra, in the three realms and the six classes of beings. Knowing that those wanderers who are mistaken about the path do not escape from saṃsāra because they are caught in the snare of the four rivers, similarly to the example of a deer caught in a snare that does not escape, the one endowed with the wisdom that knows non-apprehension "moves about" without adhering to or depending upon anything whatsoever, like a bird flying in the sky.

The essence of the third topic, the knowledge of the bases that knows all, is the realization of the non-apprehension of the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense sources, which have become the supports for the basis and path. Because it is the basis for the arising of superimpositions and the basis for the cutting of superimpositions, it is called the knowledge of the bases. Because it cuts the root of the bases by appropriately realizing the two forms of selflessness, it is the knowledge of the bases. Regarding this, out of two aspects, the pitfall or discordant class is the knowledge of the bases of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and by illustrating and teaching its antidote to be the knowledge of the bases of the Mahāyāna, one practices in the manner of cutting off the pitfall of the inferior vehicle. There are nine phenomena that illustrate this; moreover, as it says, "Through knowledge one does not dwell in existence, / and through compassion one does not dwell in peace; / the discordant class and their antidotes, / application and its equality, / and the path of seeing of the śrāvakas and so forth; / such is asserted as the very knowledge of all." Through this, these subdivisions by minor topics are also incidentally complete; they should be known extensively elsewhere.

Regarding this from "how the hero practices" up to "moves about": Moreover, by the power of the hero, the bodhisattva, practicing in whatever way through various methods, and of the perfection of wisdom, they have perfectly transcended the two afflictions that are the causes of the three realms, yet they are not liberated in the manner of the one-sided peace of the śrāvakas. Even though the afflictions of ignorance and views are eliminated, without abandoning even the mere contaminants of desire and craving, they demonstrate birth through skillful means. Likewise for the example, even though they lack aging, sickness, and death, they demonstrate dying and transmigrating and so forth in the perception of the beings to be tamed. These wandering beings who lack such wisdom are attached to the aggregates that are the basis of name, namely the four of feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness, and the aggregate of form—they are attached to those which are like the mud of the five aggregates, difficult to emerge from. For example, just as a continuous bucket water-wheel is moved by the wind, the meaning is that they wander again and again in the wheel of saṃsāra, in the three realms and the six classes of beings. Knowing that those wanderers who are mistaken about the path do not escape from saṃsāra because they are caught in the snare of the four rivers, similarly to the example of a deer caught in a snare that does not escape, the one endowed with the wisdom that knows non-apprehension "moves about" without adhering to or depending upon anything whatsoever, like a bird flying in the sky.

Thus it is said: Regarding this from "perfectly pure practice" up to "goes without attachment": if some bodhisattva with perfectly pure practice does not practice by adhering to the object of form, and similarly does not practice by way of adhering to consciousness, perception, feeling, and volition, then practicing in that way without adherence completely abandons all attachment and aversion, and that intellect going away from attachment and adherence is the Sugatas' practice of wisdom. Practicing in that way by way of not adhering to the five aggregates as appearing to be true, that bodhisattva is skilled because they possess the momentum of training, and being brilliant by realizing the meaning, having severed attachment and adherence from their own continuum, they "go" to the stage of buddhahood without attachment and adherence even to the wandering beings of the three realms.

heading: **གནག་རྫིའི་དཔེ་བསྟན་པ།**
translation: Regarding this from "the wilderness path" up to "not on the level": Similarly to the example of the cowherd, when entering into thoroughly seeking awakening, whoever attains listening and so forth to this perfection of wisdom of the Victors obtains relief from the fear of the bad migrations and is without the fear of worrying about falling into [the state of] a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha. They do not train on the level of a śrāvaka arhat, and they do not train on the level of a condition-realizing pratyekabuddha.

Applying to wisdom preceded by a question: Of the two—the complete training in all aspects and the culmination training, which mainly teach meditative equipoise as the object of meditation for the method of practicing the meaning of the three knowledges—the essence of the fourth topic, the application of complete training in all aspects, is bringing the realization of the three knowledges into the domain of effort by meditating on the four causes of the dharmakāya by subsuming the three paths into objects of observation. Because the four applications are taught by way of their own essences, they do not need to be taught by illustration. Regarding this, it is taught through eleven divisions, and furthermore it is also taught by these minor topics: "The aspects along with the applications, / the qualities, faults, and characteristics, / the factors conducive to liberation and conducive to penetration, / the assembly of irreversible learners, / the equality of existence and peace, / the unsurpassed pure realms, / and the complete realization of all aspects— / this is along with skillful means." By saying this, although there is no explicit demarcation, they are implicitly complete.

translation: Thus it is said: Regarding this from "a person [seeing] the ocean" up to "I will touch": Like that example of the ocean, having fully entered the path of accomplishing sublime awakening and having known that this itself is the volume of the perfection of wisdom, the Mother of the Victors, even if they have not been prophesied to awakening by the Guides, because their own mind is in accord with what is explained here, they should regard it, thinking, "I will also touch and attain that awakening of a Buddha before a long time elapses."

Applying to wisdom preceded by a question: Of the two—the complete training in all aspects and the culmination training, which mainly teach meditative equipoise as the object of meditation for the method of practicing the meaning of the three knowledges—the essence of the fourth topic, the application of complete training in all aspects, is bringing the realization of the three knowledges into the domain of effort by meditating on the four causes of the dharmakāya by subsuming the three paths into objects of observation. Because the four applications are taught by way of their own essences, they do not need to be taught by illustration. Regarding this, it is taught through eleven divisions, and furthermore it is also taught by these minor topics: "The aspects along with the applications, / the qualities, faults, and characteristics, / the factors conducive to liberation and conducive to penetration, / the assembly of irreversible learners, / the equality of existence and peace, / the unsurpassed pure realms, / and the complete realization of all aspects— / this is along with skillful means." By saying this, although there is no explicit demarcation, they are implicitly complete.

Applying to wisdom preceded by a question: Of the two—the complete training in all aspects and the culmination training, which mainly teach meditative equipoise as the object of meditation for the method of practicing the meaning of the three knowledges—the essence of the fourth topic, the application of complete training in all aspects, is bringing the realization of the three knowledges into the domain of effort by meditating on the four causes of the dharmakāya by subsuming the three paths into objects of observation. Because the four applications are taught by way of their own essences, they do not need to be taught by illustration. Regarding this, it is taught through eleven divisions, and furthermore it is also taught by these minor topics: "The aspects along with the applications, / the qualities, faults, and characteristics, / the factors conducive to liberation and conducive to penetration, / the assembly of irreversible learners, / the equality of existence and peace, / the unsurpassed pure realms, / and the complete realization of all aspects— / this is along with skillful means." By saying this, although there is no explicit demarcation, they are implicitly complete.

Applying to wisdom preceded by a question: Of the two—the complete training in all aspects and the culmination training, which mainly teach meditative equipoise as the object of meditation for the method of practicing the meaning of the three knowledges—the essence of the fourth topic, the application of complete training in all aspects, is bringing the realization of the three knowledges into the domain of effort by meditating on the four causes of the dharmakāya by subsuming the three paths into objects of observation. Because the four applications are taught by way of their own essences, they do not need to be taught by illustration. Regarding this, it is taught through eleven divisions, and furthermore it is also taught by these minor topics: "The aspects along with the applications, / the qualities, faults, and characteristics, / the factors conducive to liberation and conducive to penetration, / the assembly of irreversible learners, / the equality of existence and peace, / the unsurpassed pure realms, / and the complete realization of all aspects— / this is along with skillful means." By saying this, although there is no explicit demarcation, they are implicitly complete.

Because the four applications are taught by way of their own essences, they do not need to be taught by illustration. Regarding this, it is taught through eleven divisions, and furthermore it is also taught by these minor topics: "The aspects along with the applications, / the qualities, faults, and characteristics, / the factors conducive to liberation and conducive to penetration, / the assembly of irreversible learners, / the equality of existence and peace, / the unsurpassed pure realms, / and the complete realization of all aspects— / this is along with skillful means." By saying this, although there is no explicit demarcation, they are implicitly complete.

Applying to wisdom preceded by a question: Of the two—the complete training in all aspects and the culmination training, which mainly teach meditative equipoise as the object of meditation for the method of practicing the meaning of the three knowledges—the essence of the fourth topic, the application of complete training in all aspects, is bringing the realization of the three knowledges into the domain of effort by meditating on the four causes of the dharmakāya by subsuming the three paths into objects of observation. Because the four applications are taught by way of their own essences, they do not need to be taught by illustration. Regarding this, it is taught through eleven divisions, and furthermore it is also taught by these minor topics: "The aspects along with the applications, / the qualities, faults, and characteristics, / the factors conducive to liberation and conducive to penetration, / the assembly of irreversible learners, / the equality of existence and peace, / the unsurpassed pure realms, / and the complete realization of all aspects— / this is along with skillful means." By saying this, although there is no explicit demarcation, they are implicitly complete.

heading: **རྣམ་པར་མི་རྟོག་པ་བསྟན་པ།**
translation: Thus it is said: Regarding this from "whoever practices here" up to "practices the supreme perfection": For the bodhisattva who practices here in the Mother, by having practiced, they do not conceptualize the qualities of a Buddha in the manner of apprehending them as objects to be adopted. If one asks what qualities, they do not conceptualize the ten powers, the four bases of miraculous power, and the result, peaceful awakening, as the dharmakāya. They do not conceptualize them as intrinsic nature; in particular, practicing the very freedom from conceptualization through the blessings of the Buddha—this is practicing the supreme Mother, the perfection of wisdom.

Because the four applications are taught by way of their own essences, they do not need to be taught by illustration. heading: **དོན་དགོད་པ།**
translation: Regarding this from "if a mother falls ill" up to "hold in mind": Demonstrating the reasoning for this guarding by way of an example: for example, if a mother falls ill, and has many sons, when that mother falls ill, all those sons, thinking "This mother of ours is very kind," become unhappy, and in order to ensure that absolutely no harm comes to her, they attend upon that mother. Just like that example, the Buddhas of the worldly realms in the ten directions also hold in mind this supreme perfection of wisdom, which is their own mother, and therefore they guard and protect those who practice it.

translation: Thus it is said: Regarding this from "wise ones in the world" up to "name is bestowed": Furthermore, whether the wise ones, the Buddhas, abide in the world or have passed into nirvāṇa, this flawless reality, the emptiness that is the nature of phenomena, has abided from the very beginning, because the Great Sūtra says, "Whether Buddhas appear in the world or do not appear, the defining characteristic of phenomena remains just so." Because bodhisattvas, depending on the perfection of wisdom, subsequently realize this suchness in accordance with its abiding nature, the one who realizes it is also bestowed this synonym of the Buddha's name, "Tathāgata."

Thus it is said: Regarding this from "teachers of the world" up to "known by the Thus Gone": Furthermore, by this perfection of wisdom, because they awaken and show the nature of the world as it is, they are called "Victors." Likewise, it also shows the latent tendencies of sentient beings and the conduct of sentient beings themselves. As for showing reality as it is, it is the suchness of the worlds, the suchness of the noble arhats, the suchness of the pratyekabuddhas, and the suchness of the Victor's sons, the bodhisattvas. All of these are of a single nature. Where is it single? Free from entities and not other, those eight profound things, suchness and so forth, are known just as they are by the Tathāgata by relying on the path, the perfection of wisdom.

Thus it is said: Regarding this from "wise ones in the world" up to "name is bestowed": Furthermore, whether the wise ones, the Buddhas, abide in the world or have passed into nirvāṇa, this flawless reality, the emptiness that is the nature of phenomena, has abided from the very beginning, because the Great Sūtra says, "Whether Buddhas appear in the world or do not appear, the defining characteristic of phenomena remains just so." Because bodhisattvas, depending on the perfection of wisdom, subsequently realize this suchness in accordance with its abiding nature, the one who realizes it is also bestowed this synonym of the Buddha's name, "Tathāgata."

Thus it is said: Regarding this from "teachers of the world" up to "known by the Thus Gone": Furthermore, by this perfection of wisdom, because they awaken and show the nature of the world as it is, they are called "Victors." Likewise, it also shows the latent tendencies of sentient beings and the conduct of sentient beings themselves. As for showing reality as it is, it is the suchness of the worlds, the suchness of the noble arhats, the suchness of the pratyekabuddhas, and the suchness of the Victor's sons, the bodhisattvas. All of these are of a single nature. Where is it single? Free from entities and not other, those eight profound things, suchness and so forth, are known just as they are by the Tathāgata by relying on the path, the perfection of wisdom.

ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། མཁས་པ་འཇིག་རྟེན་ཞེས་པ་ནས། མཚན་གསོལ་ཏོ་ཞེས་པའི་བར་ལ། ཡང་མཁས་པ་སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་འཇིག་རྟེན་ན་གནས་སམ་འོན་ཏེ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་ཀྱང་རུང་སྟེ། ཆོས་ཉིད་ལ་ཡང་སྐྱོན་མེད་པ་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་འདི་ཡེ་ནས་གནས་ཏེ། མདོ་ཆེན་མོ་ལས་སངས་རྒྱས་འཇིག་རྟེན་དུ་བྱོན་ཡང་རུང་མ་བྱོན་ཡང་རུང་སྟེ། ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་གནས་སོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གནས་ལུགས་དེ་ལྟར་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་རྟེན་ནས་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་འདི་རྗེས་སུ་རྟོགས་པ་དེའི་ཕྱིར་རྟོགས་པ་པོ་ལ་ཡང་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མཚན་གྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་གསོལ་ཏོ། །

Thus it is said: Regarding this from "wise ones in the world" up to "name is bestowed": Furthermore, whether the wise ones, the Buddhas, abide in the world or have passed into nirvāṇa, this flawless reality, the emptiness that is the nature of phenomena, has abided from the very beginning, because the Great Sūtra says, "Whether Buddhas appear in the world or do not appear, the defining characteristic of phenomena remains just so." Because bodhisattvas, depending on the perfection of wisdom, subsequently realize this suchness in accordance with its abiding nature, the one who realizes it is also bestowed this synonym of the Buddha's name, "Tathāgata."

heading: **རྒྱས་པར་བཤད་པ།**
translation: Thus it is said: Regarding this from "suffering of sentient beings" up to "excellently teaches the Dharma": Although, generally, relatively they liberate sentient beings from suffering and, particularly, completely extract them from the three lower realms, those Guides never ultimately undergo any shift in perception, such as thinking, "I have accomplished the benefit of however many sentient beings." As for the example of overcoming false conceptions, like a human lion: just as a human lion, a Buddha, by relying on the perfection of wisdom, which is like a mountain valley, terrifies many tīrthikas who hold to wrong paths, and proclaims the sound of the emptiness of the world. As for the example of the sun for caring for others who have not realized: just like that, the Dharma King also, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, which is like the sky, dries up the water and wind of the body and enjoyments that propagate the seeds of existence, and excellently teaches the Dharma of the path to liberation.

Thus it is said: Regarding this from "wise ones in the world" up to "name is bestowed": Furthermore, whether the wise ones, the Buddhas, abide in the world or have passed into nirvāṇa, this flawless reality, the emptiness that is the nature of phenomena, has abided from the very beginning, because the Great Sūtra says, "Whether Buddhas appear in the world or do not appear, the defining characteristic of phenomena remains just so." Because bodhisattvas, depending on the perfection of wisdom, subsequently realize this suchness in accordance with its abiding nature, the one who realizes it is also bestowed this synonym of the Buddha's name, "Tathāgata."

heading: **མདོར་བསྟན་པ།**
translation: Regarding this from "forms are not seen" up to "taught by the Thus Gone": Furthermore, if sought by an examining intellect, "forms are not seen" even as mere appearances; and "feelings are not seen"; "likewise, neither is perception seen, nor is volition seen"; as for the essence of the object, from what it is accumulated, "consciousness and thinking" act as the support for knowing the mind, and because those are not seen, the unconditioned that is the opposite of them is also not seen. Therefore, this is "taught by the Thus Gone" as "seeing the reality of phenomena"; and the Sūtra that Perfectly Gathers the Dharma also teaches, "Not seeing anything at all is seeing reality."

heading: **རྒྱས་པར་བཤད་པ།**
translation: Thus it is said: By this from "seeing space" up to "sees all phenomena": If one asks, "Then how is it seen?" taking the example where some sentient beings exclaim in words, "I see space!", investigate the meaning of this seeing: "How does one see space?" If one looks in that way, it is not seen anywhere. Thus, seeing the reality of phenomena is "taught by the Thus Gone" to be like space. The example for seeing reality cannot be expressed and taught by anything other than space. Whatever bodhisattva "sees" in that manner of the non-seeing of space, that one "sees all phenomena."

Likewise, it also shows the latent tendencies of sentient beings and the conduct of sentient beings themselves. As for showing reality as it is, it is the suchness of the worlds, the suchness of the noble arhats, the suchness of the pratyekabuddhas, and the suchness of the Victor's sons, the bodhisattvas. Thus it is said: Regarding this from "wise ones in the world" up to "name is bestowed": Furthermore, whether the wise ones, the Buddhas, abide in the world or have passed into nirvāṇa, this flawless reality, the emptiness that is the nature of phenomena, has abided from the very beginning, because the Great Sūtra says, "Whether Buddhas appear in the world or do not appear, the defining characteristic of phenomena remains just so." translation: Thus it is said: Regarding this from "king equanimous" up to "perfection performs": For example, just as a great king sits in equanimity while his appointed ministers perform all the affairs of the kingdom, the bodhisattva's buddha-activities and however many qualities of the śrāvakas there are, all of those are also performed by the perfection of wisdom, which is like the minister.

Likewise, it also shows the latent tendencies of sentient beings and the conduct of sentient beings themselves. heading: **རྒྱལ་པོའི་དཔེས་བྱ་བ་རྨད་དུ་བྱུང་བ་དང་ལྡན་པ།**
translation: Thus it is said: Regarding this from "king into the village" up to "gathers all": Furthermore, for example, when a great king gathers taxes, he does not go into the village, nor does he go into the province; staying in his own place, all the gatherings of taxes and so forth are gathered by his minister. Just so, the bodhisattva, at the time of meditative equipoise, does not go anywhere in reality, and at the time of post-meditation, whatever qualities of the Buddha's ground there are, such as the powers and fearlessnesses, are all gathered.

Thus it is said: Regarding this from "king into the village" up to "gathers all": Furthermore, for example, when a great king gathers taxes, he does not go into the village, nor does he go into the province; staying in his own place, all the gatherings of taxes and so forth are gathered by his minister. Just so, the bodhisattva, at the time of meditative equipoise, does not go anywhere in reality, and at the time of post-meditation, whatever qualities of the Buddha's ground there are, such as the powers and fearlessnesses, are all gathered.

heading: **མདོར་བསྟན་པ།**
translation: Regarding this from "in whoever the Sugata" up to "quickly attains": Because whatever bodhisattva has a heroic mind toward the awakening realized by the Sugata and has stable faith, and because they have intention and application toward the supreme perfection of wisdom, they have coupled means and wisdom. Because of that, having greatly transcended the two grounds of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, their continuum is not overwhelmed by all the obscurations, and they quickly attain the unsurpassed awakening of a Conqueror.

As for the example of the sun for caring for others who have not realized: just like that, the Dharma King also, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, which is like the sky, dries up the water and wind of the body and enjoyments that propagate the seeds of existence, and excellently teaches the Dharma of the path to liberation.

གཟུགས་རྣམས་མི་མཐོང་ངོ་ཞེས་པ་ནས། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བསྟན་ཞེས་པའི་བར་ལ། ཡང་རྣམ་པར་སྤྱོད་པའི་བློས་བཙལ་ན་གཟུགས་རྣམས་སྣང་ཙམ་དུ་ཡང་མི་མཐོང་ཞིང༌། ཚོར་བ་དག་ཀྱང་མི་མཐོང་ཞིང༌། དེ་བཞིན་འདུ་ཤེས་ཀྱང་མཐོང་བ་མེད་ལ་སེམས་པ་ཡང་མི་མཐོང་ཞིང༌། དོན་གྱི་ངོ་བོ་ལ་གང་ལ་བསགས་པ་ནས། རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་དང་བསམས་པས་ན་སེམས་ཤེས་པའི་རྟེན་བྱེད་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་རྣམས་མཐོང་བ་མེད་པས་དེ་རྣམས་ལས་བཟློག་པའི་འདུས་མ་བྱས་ཀྱང་མཐོང་བ་མེད་པས་ཏེ། འདི་ནི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐོང་བ་ཡིན་ཞེས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བསྟན་པ་དང༌། ཆོས་ཡང་དག་པར་བསྡུས་པའི་མདོ་ལས་ཀྱང་འགའ་ཡང་མཐོང་བ་མེད་པ་ནི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་མཐོང་ཞེས་བསྟན་ཏོ། །

Regarding this from "forms are not seen" up to "taught by the Thus Gone": Furthermore, if sought by an examining intellect, "forms are not seen" even as mere appearances; and "feelings are not seen"; "likewise, neither is perception seen, nor is volition seen"; as for the essence of the object, from what it is accumulated, "consciousness and thinking" act as the support for knowing the mind, and because those are not seen, the unconditioned that is the opposite of them is also not seen. Therefore, this is "taught by the Thus Gone" as "seeing the reality of phenomena"; and the Sūtra that Perfectly Gathers the Dharma also teaches, "Not seeing anything at all is seeing reality."

[2-129] source:
ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། ནམ་མཁའ་མཐོང་ཞེས་པ་ནས། ཆོས་ཀུན་མཐོང་ཞེས་པའི་བར་གྱིས། འོ་ན་ཇི་ལྟར་མཐོང་ཞེ་ན་དཔེ་ནམ་མཁའ་མཐོང་ངོ་ཞེས་སེམས་ཅན་ཁ་ཅིག་གིས་ཚིག་གིས་རབ་ཏུ་བརྗོད་པ་དེ་དག་གི་དོན། ནམ་མཁའ་ཇི་ལྟར་མཐོང་སྟེ་མཐོང་བའི་དོན་འདི་བརྟག་པར་གྱིས། དེ་ལྟར་བལྟས་ན་གང་དུ་ཡང་མཐོང་བ་མེད་པ། དེ་ལྟར་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐོང་བ་ཡང་ནམ་མཁའ་ལྟ་བུར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐོང་བའི་དཔེ་ནམ་མཁའ་ལས་གཞན་གྱིས་ཀྱང་ནི་བསྙད་ཅིང་བསྟན་པར་ནུས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་གིས་ནམ་མཁའ་མཐོང་མེད་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་དེ་ལྟར་མཐོང་བ་དེ་ཡིས་ཆོས་ཀུན་ཀྱང་མཐོང་ངོ༌། །

Thus it is said: By this from "seeing space" up to "sees all phenomena": If one asks, "Then how is it seen?" taking the example where some sentient beings exclaim in words, "I see space!", investigate the meaning of this seeing: "How does one see space?" If one looks in that way, it is not seen anywhere. Thus, seeing the reality of phenomena is "taught by the Thus Gone" to be like space. The example for seeing reality cannot be expressed and taught by anything other than space. Whatever bodhisattva "sees" in that manner of the non-seeing of space, that one "sees all phenomena."

Thus it is said: Regarding this from "king equanimous" up to "perfection performs": For example, just as a great king sits in equanimity while his appointed ministers perform all the affairs of the kingdom, the bodhisattva's buddha-activities and however many qualities of the śrāvakas there are, all of those are also performed by the perfection of wisdom, which is like the minister.

[2-131] source:
ཅེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། རྒྱལ་པོ་གྲོང་དུ་ཞེས་པ་ནས། ཐམས་ཅད་བསྡུས་ཞེས་པའི་བར་ལ། ཡང་དཔེར་ན་རྒྱལ་པོ་ཆེན་པོ་བཅའ་བསྡུས་པ་ལའང་གྲོང་དུ་ཡང་མི་འགྲོ་ལ་ཡུལ་འཁོར་དུ་ཡང་མི་འགྲོ་བར། རང་གི་ཡུལ་དུ་འདུག་ནས་བཅའ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་འདུ་བ་ཐམས་ཅད་བློན་པོས་བསྡུས་པ་ལྟར་དུ། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་མཉམ་བཞག་གི་དུས་ན་ཆོས་ཉིད་གང་དུ་ཡང་མི་འགྲོ་ལ། རྗེས་ཐོབ་ཀྱི་དུས་ན་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སའི་ཡོན་ཏན་སྟོབས་དང་མི་འཇིགས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་གང་ཡིན་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་བསྡུས་པའོ། །
[2-131] translation already produced for this document:
Thus it is said: Regarding this from "king into the village" up to "gathers all": Furthermore, for example, when a great king gathers taxes, he does not go into the village, nor does he go into the province; staying in his own place, all the gatherings of taxes and so forth are gathered by his minister. Just so, the bodhisattva, at the time of meditative equipoise, does not go anywhere in reality, and at the time of post-meditation, whatever qualities of the Buddha's ground there are, such as the powers and fearlessnesses, are all gathered.

Thus it is said: Regarding this from "suffering of sentient beings" up to "excellently teaches the Dharma": Although, generally, relatively they liberate sentient beings from suffering and, particularly, completely extract them from the three lower realms, those Guides never ultimately undergo any shift in perception, such as thinking, "I have accomplished the benefit of however many sentient beings." As for the example of overcoming false conceptions, like a human lion: just as a human lion, a Buddha, by relying on the perfection of wisdom, which is like a mountain valley, terrifies many tīrthikas who hold to wrong paths, and proclaims the sound of the emptiness of the world. As for the example of the sun for caring for others who have not realized: just like that, the Dharma King also, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, which is like the sky, dries up the water and wind of the body and enjoyments that propagate the seeds of existence, and excellently teaches the Dharma of the path to liberation.

If one looks in that way, it is not seen anywhere. Thus, seeing the reality of phenomena is "taught by the Thus Gone" to be like space. The example for seeing reality cannot be expressed and taught by anything other than space. Whatever bodhisattva "sees" in that manner of the non-seeing of space, that one "sees all phenomena."

Thus it is said: Regarding this from "king into the village" up to "gathers all": Furthermore, for example, when a great king gathers taxes, he does not go into the village, nor does he go into the province; staying in his own place, all the gatherings of taxes and so forth are gathered by his minister. Just so, the bodhisattva, at the time of meditative equipoise, does not go anywhere in reality, and at the time of post-meditation, whatever qualities of the Buddha's ground there are, such as the powers and fearlessnesses, are all gathered.

heading: **རྒྱ་མཚོའི་གྲུ་ཞིག་པ་འཛིན་པ་དང་མི་འཛིན་པའི་དཔེ།**
translation: Regarding this from "for example, entering the ocean" up to "quickly touches": As for the example of grasping to attachment and not grasping: just so, whatever bodhisattva is endowed with faith in the cause and has attained faith in the result, if they do not follow the Mother, the perfection of wisdom, together with means, they will not attain awakening. If those who are endowed with faith are thoroughly embraced by wisdom right when they are endowed with the qualities of means that desire the benefit of sentient beings, they will quickly touch the awakening of the Sugatas, which is supremely wonderful in qualities.

As for the example of overcoming false conceptions, like a human lion: just as a human lion, a Buddha, by relying on the perfection of wisdom, which is like a mountain valley, terrifies many tīrthikas who hold to wrong paths, and proclaims the sound of the emptiness of the world. As for the example of the sun for caring for others who have not realized: just like that, the Dharma King also, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, which is like the sky, dries up the water and wind of the body and enjoyments that propagate the seeds of existence, and excellently teaches the Dharma of the path to liberation.

གཟུགས་རྣམས་མི་མཐོང་ངོ་ཞེས་པ་ནས། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བསྟན་ཞེས་པའི་བར་ལ། ཡང་རྣམ་པར་སྤྱོད་པའི་བློས་བཙལ་ན་གཟུགས་རྣམས་སྣང་ཙམ་དུ་ཡང་མི་མཐོང་ཞིང༌། ཚོར་བ་དག་ཀྱང་མི་མཐོང་ཞིང༌། དེ་བཞིན་འདུ་ཤེས་ཀྱང་མཐོང་བ་མེད་ལ་སེམས་པ་ཡང་མི་མཐོང་ཞིང༌། དོན་གྱི་ངོ་བོ་ལ་གང་ལ་བསགས་པ་ནས། རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་དང་བསམས་པས་ན་སེམས་ཤེས་པའི་རྟེན་བྱེད་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་རྣམས་མཐོང་བ་མེད་པས་དེ་རྣམས་ལས་བཟློག་པའི་འདུས་མ་བྱས་ཀྱང་མཐོང་བ་མེད་པས་ཏེ། འདི་ནི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐོང་བ་ཡིན་ཞེས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བསྟན་པ་དང༌། ཆོས་ཡང་དག་པར་བསྡུས་པའི་མདོ་ལས་ཀྱང་འགའ་ཡང་མཐོང་བ་མེད་པ་ནི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་མཐོང་ཞེས་བསྟན་ཏོ། །

Regarding this from "forms are not seen" up to "taught by the Thus Gone": Furthermore, if sought by an examining intellect, "forms are not seen" even as mere appearances; and "feelings are not seen"; "likewise, neither is perception seen, nor is volition seen"; as for the essence of the object, from what it is accumulated, "consciousness and thinking" act as the support for knowing the mind, and because those are not seen, the unconditioned that is the opposite of them is also not seen. Therefore, this is "taught by the Thus Gone" as "seeing the reality of phenomena"; and the Sūtra that Perfectly Gathers the Dharma also teaches, "Not seeing anything at all is seeing reality."

[2-129] source:
ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། ནམ་མཁའ་མཐོང་ཞེས་པ་ནས། ཆོས་ཀུན་མཐོང་ཞེས་པའི་བར་གྱིས། འོ་ན་ཇི་ལྟར་མཐོང་ཞེ་ན་དཔེ་ནམ་མཁའ་མཐོང་ངོ་ཞེས་སེམས་ཅན་ཁ་ཅིག་གིས་ཚིག་གིས་རབ་ཏུ་བརྗོད་པ་དེ་དག་གི་དོན། ནམ་མཁའ་ཇི་ལྟར་མཐོང་སྟེ་མཐོང་བའི་དོན་འདི་བརྟག་པར་གྱིས། དེ་ལྟར་བལྟས་ན་གང་དུ་ཡང་མཐོང་བ་མེད་པ། དེ་ལྟར་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐོང་བ་ཡང་ནམ་མཁའ་ལྟ་བུར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐོང་བའི་དཔེ་ནམ་མཁའ་ལས་གཞན་གྱིས་ཀྱང་ནི་བསྙད་ཅིང་བསྟན་པར་ནུས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་གིས་ནམ་མཁའ་མཐོང་མེད་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་དེ་ལྟར་མཐོང་བ་དེ་ཡིས་ཆོས་ཀུན་ཀྱང་མཐོང་ངོ༌། །

Thus it is said: By this from "seeing space" up to "sees all phenomena": If one asks, "Then how is it seen?" taking the example where some sentient beings exclaim in words, "I see space!", investigate the meaning of this seeing: "How does one see space?" If one looks in that way, it is not seen anywhere. Thus, seeing the reality of phenomena is "taught by the Thus Gone" to be like space. The example for seeing reality cannot be expressed and taught by anything other than space. Whatever bodhisattva "sees" in that manner of the non-seeing of space, that one "sees all phenomena."

[2-130] source:
ཅེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། རྒྱལ་པོ་བཏང་སྙོམས་ཞེས་པ་ནས། ཕྱིན་པ་བྱེད་ཞེས་པའི་བར་ལ། དཔེར་ན་རྒྱལ་པོ་ཆེན་པོ་སྟེ་བཏང་སྙོམས་སུ་འདུག་ཅིང་ལས་བྱེད་དུ་བཅུག་པའི་བློན་པོས་རྒྱལ་སྲིད་ཀྱི་བྱ་བ་ཀུན་བྱེད་པ་ལྟར། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མཛད་པ་དང་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཇི་སྙེད་པ་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་བློན་པོ་ལྟ་བུའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པས་བྱེད་དོ། །

Thus it is said: Regarding this from "king equanimous" up to "perfection performs": For example, just as a great king sits in equanimity while his appointed ministers perform all the affairs of the kingdom, the bodhisattva's buddha-activities and however many qualities of the śrāvakas there are, all of those are also performed by the perfection of wisdom, which is like the minister.

[2-131] source:
ཅེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། རྒྱལ་པོ་གྲོང་དུ་ཞེས་པ་ནས། ཐམས་ཅད་བསྡུས་ཞེས་པའི་བར་ལ། ཡང་དཔེར་ན་རྒྱལ་པོ་ཆེན་པོ་བཅའ་བསྡུས་པ་ལའང་གྲོང་དུ་ཡང་མི་འགྲོ་ལ་ཡུལ་འཁོར་དུ་ཡང་མི་འགྲོ་བར། རང་གི་ཡུལ་དུ་འདུག་ནས་བཅའ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་འདུ་བ་ཐམས་ཅད་བློན་པོས་བསྡུས་པ་ལྟར་དུ། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་མཉམ་བཞག་གི་དུས་ན་ཆོས་ཉིད་གང་དུ་ཡང་མི་འགྲོ་ལ། རྗེས་ཐོབ་ཀྱི་དུས་ན་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སའི་ཡོན་ཏན་སྟོབས་དང་མི་འཇིགས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་གང་ཡིན་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་བསྡུས་པའོ། །
[2-131] translation already produced for this document:
Thus it is said: Regarding this from "king into the village" up to "gathers all": Furthermore, for example, when a great king gathers taxes, he does not go into the village, nor does he go into the province; staying in his own place, all the gatherings of taxes and so forth are gathered by his minister. Just so, the bodhisattva, at the time of meditative equipoise, does not go anywhere in reality, and at the time of post-meditation, whatever qualities of the Buddha's ground there are, such as the powers and fearlessnesses, are all gathered.

heading: **བུམ་པ་སོ་བཏང་བ་དང་མ་བཏང་པའི་དཔེ།**
translation: Thus it is said: Regarding this from "for example, someone" up to "attains the supreme": Just as in the example of the unfired and fired clay vessel, even if a bodhisattva has much faith, such as conviction in cause and effect, if they are completely bereft of the wisdom that knows non-apprehension, they will fall into saṃsāra and thus quickly become ruined from the path of liberation. If, with faith, they are thoroughly embraced by that wisdom of non-apprehension, they will greatly transcend the two grounds of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and attain unsurpassed awakening.

Thus it is said: Regarding this from "suffering of sentient beings" up to "excellently teaches the Dharma": Although, generally, relatively they liberate sentient beings from suffering and, particularly, completely extract them from the three lower realms, those Guides never ultimately undergo any shift in perception, such as thinking, "I have accomplished the benefit of however many sentient beings." As for the example of overcoming false conceptions, like a human lion: just as a human lion, a Buddha, by relying on the perfection of wisdom, which is like a mountain valley, terrifies many tīrthikas who hold to wrong paths, and proclaims the sound of the emptiness of the world. As for the example of the sun for caring for others who have not realized: just like that, the Dharma King also, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, which is like the sky, dries up the water and wind of the body and enjoyments that propagate the seeds of existence, and excellently teaches the Dharma of the path to liberation.

If one looks in that way, it is not seen anywhere. Thus, seeing the reality of phenomena is "taught by the Thus Gone" to be like space. Thus it is said: Regarding this from "king into the village" up to "gathers all": Furthermore, for example, when a great king gathers taxes, he does not go into the village, nor does he go into the province; staying in his own place, all the gatherings of taxes and so forth are gathered by his minister. Just so, the bodhisattva, at the time of meditative equipoise, does not go anywhere in reality, and at the time of post-meditation, whatever qualities of the Buddha's ground there are, such as the powers and fearlessnesses, are all gathered.

heading: **ཆུ་རྒལ་བའི་གྲུ་མ་བཅོས་པ་དང་བཅོས་པའི་དཔེ།**
translation: Thus it is said: Regarding this from "for example, well-built" up to "will touch": Just as in the example of an unbuilt and built ship entering the ocean, the meaning is that even if a bodhisattva's continuum is thoroughly infused with faith, if they lack natural wisdom, they will quickly deteriorate from attaining perfect awakening. If that very one with faith possesses the realization of the supreme perfection of wisdom, furthermore, not being wounded by the afflictive obscurations of the inferior, and not deteriorating by the cognitive obscurations of conceit, they will touch and attain the awakening of a Conqueror.

Thus it is said: Regarding this from "king into the village" up to "gathers all": Furthermore, for example, when a great king gathers taxes, he does not go into the village, nor does he go into the province; staying in his own place, all the gatherings of taxes and so forth are gathered by his minister. heading: **རྒད་པོ་འདོད་པ་བརྟན་མི་ཡོད་པ་དང་མེད་པའི་དཔེ།**
translation: Thus it is said: Regarding this from "reached one hundred and twenty years" up to "will touch": Just like the example of the old man, even if a bodhisattva, merely having weak power of the intellect—the wisdom that realizes selflessness—has initially excellently entered through faith, they will quickly deteriorate in the interim. If that very one with faith knows the means of great compassion and supreme wisdom as non-apprehension, and is thoroughly embraced by both of them, they will not deteriorate by conditions in the interim, but will touch the awakening of the Thus Gone.

གཟུགས་རྣམས་མི་མཐོང་ངོ་ཞེས་པ་ནས། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བསྟན་ཞེས་པའི་བར་ལ། ཡང་རྣམ་པར་སྤྱོད་པའི་བློས་བཙལ་ན་གཟུགས་རྣམས་སྣང་ཙམ་དུ་ཡང་མི་མཐོང་ཞིང༌། ཚོར་བ་དག་ཀྱང་མི་མཐོང་ཞིང༌། དེ་བཞིན་འདུ་ཤེས་ཀྱང་མཐོང་བ་མེད་ལ་སེམས་པ་ཡང་མི་མཐོང་ཞིང༌། དོན་གྱི་ངོ་བོ་ལ་གང་ལ་བསགས་པ་ནས། རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་དང་བསམས་པས་ན་སེམས་ཤེས་པའི་རྟེན་བྱེད་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་རྣམས་མཐོང་བ་མེད་པས་དེ་རྣམས་ལས་བཟློག་པའི་འདུས་མ་བྱས་ཀྱང་མཐོང་བ་མེད་པས་ཏེ། འདི་ནི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐོང་བ་ཡིན་ཞེས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བསྟན་པ་དང༌། ཆོས་ཡང་དག་པར་བསྡུས་པའི་མདོ་ལས་ཀྱང་འགའ་ཡང་མཐོང་བ་མེད་པ་ནི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་མཐོང་ཞེས་བསྟན་ཏོ། །

Regarding this from "forms are not seen" up to "taught by the Thus Gone": Furthermore, if sought by an examining intellect, "forms are not seen" even as mere appearances; and "feelings are not seen"; "likewise, neither is perception seen, nor is volition seen"; as for the essence of the object, from what it is accumulated, "consciousness and thinking" act as the support for knowing the mind, and because those are not seen, the unconditioned that is the opposite of them is also not seen. Therefore, this is "taught by the Thus Gone" as "seeing the reality of phenomena"; and the Sūtra that Perfectly Gathers the Dharma also teaches, "Not seeing anything at all is seeing reality."

Thus it is said: Regarding this from "king equanimous" up to "perfection performs": For example, just as a great king sits in equanimity while his appointed ministers perform all the affairs of the kingdom, the bodhisattva's buddha-activities and however many qualities of the śrāvakas there are, all of those are also performed by the perfection of wisdom, which is like the minister.

Thus it is said: Regarding this from "king into the village" up to "gathers all": Furthermore, for example, when a great king gathers taxes, he does not go into the village, nor does he go into the province; staying in his own place, all the gatherings of taxes and so forth are gathered by his minister. Just so, the bodhisattva, at the time of meditative equipoise, does not go anywhere in reality, and at the time of post-meditation, whatever qualities of the Buddha's ground there are, such as the powers and fearlessnesses, are all gathered.

As for the example of the sun for caring for others who have not realized: just like that, the Dharma King also, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, which is like the sky, dries up the water and wind of the body and enjoyments that propagate the seeds of existence, and excellently teaches the Dharma of the path to liberation.

གཟུགས་རྣམས་མི་མཐོང་ངོ་ཞེས་པ་ནས། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བསྟན་ཞེས་པའི་བར་ལ། ཡང་རྣམ་པར་སྤྱོད་པའི་བློས་བཙལ་ན་གཟུགས་རྣམས་སྣང་ཙམ་དུ་ཡང་མི་མཐོང་ཞིང༌། ཚོར་བ་དག་ཀྱང་མི་མཐོང་ཞིང༌། དེ་བཞིན་འདུ་ཤེས་ཀྱང་མཐོང་བ་མེད་ལ་སེམས་པ་ཡང་མི་མཐོང་ཞིང༌། དོན་གྱི་ངོ་བོ་ལ་གང་ལ་བསགས་པ་ནས། རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་དང་བསམས་པས་ན་སེམས་ཤེས་པའི་རྟེན་བྱེད་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་རྣམས་མཐོང་བ་མེད་པས་དེ་རྣམས་ལས་བཟློག་པའི་འདུས་མ་བྱས་ཀྱང་མཐོང་བ་མེད་པས་ཏེ། འདི་ནི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐོང་བ་ཡིན་ཞེས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བསྟན་པ་དང༌། ཆོས་ཡང་དག་པར་བསྡུས་པའི་མདོ་ལས་ཀྱང་འགའ་ཡང་མཐོང་བ་མེད་པ་ནི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་མཐོང་ཞེས་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[2-128] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding this from "forms are not seen" up to "taught by the Thus Gone": Furthermore, if sought by an examining intellect, "forms are not seen" even as mere appearances; and "feelings are not seen"; "likewise, neither is perception seen, nor is volition seen"; as for the essence of the object, from what it is accumulated, "consciousness and thinking" act as the support for knowing the mind, and because those are not seen, the unconditioned that is the opposite of them is also not seen. Therefore, this is "taught by the Thus Gone" as "seeing the reality of phenomena"; and the Sūtra that Perfectly Gathers the Dharma also teaches, "Not seeing anything at all is seeing reality."

[2-129] source:
ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། ནམ་མཁའ་མཐོང་ཞེས་པ་ནས། ཆོས་ཀུན་མཐོང་ཞེས་པའི་བར་གྱིས། འོ་ན་ཇི་ལྟར་མཐོང་ཞེ་ན་དཔེ་ནམ་མཁའ་མཐོང་ངོ་ཞེས་སེམས་ཅན་ཁ་ཅིག་གིས་ཚིག་གིས་རབ་ཏུ་བརྗོད་པ་དེ་དག་གི་དོན། ནམ་མཁའ་ཇི་ལྟར་མཐོང་སྟེ་མཐོང་བའི་དོན་འདི་བརྟག་པར་གྱིས། དེ་ལྟར་བལྟས་ན་གང་དུ་ཡང་མཐོང་བ་མེད་པ། དེ་ལྟར་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐོང་བ་ཡང་ནམ་མཁའ་ལྟ་བུར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐོང་བའི་དཔེ་ནམ་མཁའ་ལས་གཞན་གྱིས་ཀྱང་ནི་བསྙད་ཅིང་བསྟན་པར་ནུས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་གིས་ནམ་མཁའ་མཐོང་མེད་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་དེ་ལྟར་མཐོང་བ་དེ་ཡིས་ཆོས་ཀུན་ཀྱང་མཐོང་ངོ༌། །
[2-129] translation already produced for this document:
Thus it is said: By this from "seeing space" up to "sees all phenomena": If one asks, "Then how is it seen?" taking the example where some sentient beings exclaim in words, "I see space!", investigate the meaning of this seeing: "How does one see space?" If one looks in that way, it is not seen anywhere. Thus, seeing the reality of phenomena is "taught by the Thus Gone" to be like space. The example for seeing reality cannot be expressed and taught by anything other than space. Whatever bodhisattva "sees" in that manner of the non-seeing of space, that one "sees all phenomena."

[2-130] source:
ཅེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། རྒྱལ་པོ་བཏང་སྙོམས་ཞེས་པ་ནས། ཕྱིན་པ་བྱེད་ཞེས་པའི་བར་ལ། དཔེར་ན་རྒྱལ་པོ་ཆེན་པོ་སྟེ་བཏང་སྙོམས་སུ་འདུག་ཅིང་ལས་བྱེད་དུ་བཅུག་པའི་བློན་པོས་རྒྱལ་སྲིད་ཀྱི་བྱ་བ་ཀུན་བྱེད་པ་ལྟར། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མཛད་པ་དང་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཇི་སྙེད་པ་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་བློན་པོ་ལྟ་བུའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པས་བྱེད་དོ། །
[2-130] translation already produced for this document:
Thus it is said: Regarding this from "king equanimous" up to "perfection performs": For example, just as a great king sits in equanimity while his appointed ministers perform all the affairs of the kingdom, the bodhisattva's buddha-activities and however many qualities of the śrāvakas there are, all of those are also performed by the perfection of wisdom, which is like the minister.

[2-131] source:
ཅེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། རྒྱལ་པོ་གྲོང་དུ་ཞེས་པ་ནས། ཐམས་ཅད་བསྡུས་ཞེས་པའི་བར་ལ། ཡང་དཔེར་ན་རྒྱལ་པོ་ཆེན་པོ་བཅའ་བསྡུས་པ་ལའང་གྲོང་དུ་ཡང་མི་འགྲོ་ལ་ཡུལ་འཁོར་དུ་ཡང་མི་འགྲོ་བར། རང་གི་ཡུལ་དུ་འདུག་ནས་བཅའ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་འདུ་བ་ཐམས་ཅད་བློན་པོས་བསྡུས་པ་ལྟར་དུ། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་མཉམ་བཞག་གི་དུས་ན་ཆོས་ཉིད་གང་དུ་ཡང་མི་འགྲོ་ལ། རྗེས་ཐོབ་ཀྱི་དུས་ན་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སའི་ཡོན་ཏན་སྟོབས་དང་མི་འཇིགས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་གང་ཡིན་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་བསྡུས་པའོ། །
[2-131] translation already produced for this document:
Thus it is said: Regarding this from "king into the village" up to "gathers all": Furthermore, for example, when a great king gathers taxes, he does not go into the village, nor does he go into the province; staying in his own place, all the gatherings of taxes and so forth are gathered by his minister. Just so, the bodhisattva, at the time of meditative equipoise, does not go anywhere in reality, and at the time of post-meditation, whatever qualities of the Buddha's ground there are, such as the powers and fearlessnesses, are all gathered.

heading: **སྟེན་པ་པོ་སློབ་མའི་མཚན་ཉིད།**
translation: Regarding this from "bodhisattva" up to "by them": As for the circumstantial distinction of bodhisattvas, whatever beginners abiding on the ground of preliminary practices, out of the superior intention desiring awakening for the benefit of others, enter into the supreme awakening of a Buddha; as for the essential distinction, by being endowed with devotion to the guru like the good disciple Sadāprarudita and like Sudhana, they will attain the perfect path.

[2-134] translation already produced for this document:
Thus it is said:

[2-135] source:
དཔེར་ན་རྒྱ་མཚོར་འཇུག་ཞེས་པ་ནས། མྱུར་དུ་རེག་ཞེས་པའི་བར་ལ། ཆགས་པ་འཛིན་པ་དང༌། མི་འཛིན་པའི་དཔེ་དེ་ལྟར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྒྱུ་ལ་དད་པ་དང་ལྡན་ཞིང་འབྲས་བུ་ལ་དད་པའི་དད་པ་ཐོབ་པ་གང་ལ་ལ་ཞིག་ནི། ཐབས་དང་བཅས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་ཡུམ་གྱི་རྗེས་སུ་མི་འབྱུང་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པ་མིན་ལ། དད་པ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དེ་དག་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་དོན་འདོད་པའི་ཐབས་ཀྱི་ཡོན་ཏན་དང་ལྡན་པ་དེ་ཉིད་དུ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཟིན་ན། ཡོན་ཏན་མཆོག་ཏུ་རྨད་དུ་བྱུང་བའི་བདེར་གཤེགས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ལ་མྱུར་དུ་རེག་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[2-135] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding this from "for example, entering the ocean" up to "quickly touches": As for the example of grasping to attachment and not grasping: just so, whatever bodhisattva is endowed with faith in the cause and has attained faith in the result, if they do not follow the Mother, the perfection of wisdom, together with means, they will not attain awakening. If those who are endowed with faith are thoroughly embraced by wisdom right when they are endowed with the qualities of means that desire the benefit of sentient beings, they will quickly touch the awakening of the Sugatas, which is supremely wonderful in qualities.

[2-136] source:
ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། དཔེར་ན་ལ་ལ་ཞེས་པ་ནས། མཆོག་ཐོབ་གྱུར་ཞེས་པའི་བར་ལ། རྫ་སོ་བཏང་བ་དང་མ་བཏང་བའི་དཔེ་བཞིན་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྒྱུ་འབྲས་ལ་ཡིད་ཆེས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དད་པ་མང་པོ་ཡོད་པར་གྱུར་ཀྱང༌། མི་དམིགས་པར་ཤེས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་རྣམ་པར་ཉམས་ན་འཁོར་བར་ལྟུང་བས་ཐར་ལམ་ལས་མྱུར་དུ་མ་རུངས་པར་གྱུར་ལ། དད་པས་དེ་ཉིད་མི་དམིགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་དེས་ནི་ཡོངས་སུ་ཟིན་པར་གྱུར་ན། ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་ས་དང་རང་རྒྱལ་བའི་ས་གཉིས་ལས་ཤིན་ཏུ་འདས་ཏེ་བླ་ན་མེད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[2-136] translation already produced for this document:
Thus it is said: Regarding this from "for example, someone" up to "attains the supreme": Just as in the example of the unfired and fired clay vessel, even if a bodhisattva has much faith, such as conviction in cause and effect, if they are completely bereft of the wisdom that knows non-apprehension, they will fall into saṃsāra and thus quickly become ruined from the path of liberation.
